## What you will learn

After this tutorial, you should be able to:

- choose coherent power, voltage, current, and impedance bases for a balanced three-phase system;
- propagate voltage bases across transformers and explain why nominal turns ratios then disappear;
- convert impedances and admittances between bases; and
- normalise a multi-zone network, solve it in per unit, and recover the physical values of each zone.

## Prerequisites

- Ohm's law, complex power, and line-to-line versus line-to-neutral voltage in a balanced three-phase system.
- [Complex-numbers tutorial](complex-numbers-in-ac-circuits.qmd): phasors and complex power.
- [Star--delta tutorial](star-delta-three-phase-systems.qmd): three-phase voltage and current relationships.

## 1. A per-unit value is a ratio to a declared base

A **per-unit value** is a physical quantity divided by a chosen reference value of the same kind:

$$
x_{pu}=\frac{x}{x_B},
\qquad
x=x_{pu}x_B.
$$ {#eq-pu-definition}

The result is dimensionless; the subscript $B$ denotes the base, not an operating point. A $220\ \mathrm{kV}$ voltage on a $230\ \mathrm{kV}$ base is $0.9565$ p.u. Percent values carry the same information, $x_{\%}=100x_{pu}$: an $8\%$ transformer impedance is $0.08$ p.u., not $8$ p.u.

::: {.callout-important}
A per-unit number is incomplete without its base: $1$ p.u. voltage can mean $400\ \mathrm{V}$ in one zone and $230\ \mathrm{kV}$ in another — equal normalised values, different physical voltages.
:::

## 2. Choose two bases; the rest follow

Voltage, current, power, and impedance bases cannot all be chosen independently if Ohm's law and the power equations are to keep their usual form. Power-system studies select a three-phase apparent-power base $S_B$ and a line-to-line RMS voltage base $V_B$ at one bus; the balanced relation $S=\sqrt{3}V_{LL}I_L$ then fixes

$$
I_B=\frac{S_B}{\sqrt{3}V_B},
$$ {#eq-pu-current-base}

$$
Z_B=\frac{V_B^2}{S_B},
\qquad
Y_B=\frac{1}{Z_B}=\frac{S_B}{V_B^2}.
$$ {#eq-pu-impedance-base}

With $S_B$ in MVA and $V_B$ in kV, @eq-pu-current-base gives kA and @eq-pu-impedance-base gives ohms. Per-phase quantities give the same impedance base,

$$
\frac{V_{B,LN}^2}{S_B/3}
=\frac{(V_{B,LL}/\sqrt{3})^2}{S_B/3}
=\frac{V_{B,LL}^2}{S_B},
$$ {#eq-pu-phase-three-phase-consistency}

but only when the line-to-line/line-to-neutral and total/per-phase conventions are paired consistently.

## 3. Normalisation preserves the circuit laws

In every ratio below, the numerator and its base must share the same convention: line-to-line voltage over a line-to-line base, or phase-to-neutral voltage over its phase-to-neutral base $V_{B,\phi}=V_{B,LL}/\sqrt{3}$.

| Quantity | Per-unit definition | Recover physical value |
|---|---|---|
| Voltage | $\underline V_{pu}=\underline V/V_B$ | $\underline V=\underline V_{pu}V_B$ |
| Current | $\underline I_{pu}=\underline I/I_B$ | $\underline I=\underline I_{pu}I_B$ |
| Complex power | $\underline S_{pu}=\underline S/S_B$ | $\underline S=\underline S_{pu}S_B$ |
| Impedance | $\underline Z_{pu}=\underline Z/Z_B$ | $\underline Z=\underline Z_{pu}Z_B$ |
| Admittance | $\underline Y_{pu}=\underline Y/Y_B$ | $\underline Y=\underline Y_{pu}Y_B$ |

: Per-unit and physical quantities {#tbl-pu-definitions}

Take $\underline V_\phi$ as a phase-to-neutral voltage and $\underline I$ as the corresponding line current. Because $Z_B=V_{B,\phi}/I_B$ and $S_B=3V_{B,\phi}I_B$, both governing relations keep their familiar form:

$$
\underline V_{\phi,pu}=\underline Z_{pu}\underline I_{pu},
\qquad
\underline S_{pu}=\underline V_{\phi,pu}\underline I_{pu}^*.
$$ {#eq-pu-ohms-law}

Per-unit normalisation is thus a change of numerical scale that preserves the circuit laws [@grainger1994; @ybus_glover2017]. In practice, operating points read directly as deviations from base ($0.97$ p.u. is $3\%$ low at any voltage level), impedances of very different ratings fall into comparable ranges, nominal transformer ratios drop out of multi-voltage networks, and most quantities stay near unity.

::: {.callout-note}
Angles stay in radians or degrees; they are not divided by a base. A value such as $0.95$ p.u. should also state whether it is a magnitude or a complex phasor.
:::

## 4. Why the ideal transformer ratio disappears

Consider an ideal transformer with no phase shift and rated magnitude ratio $a=V_{r,H}/V_{r,L}$. Use the same power base on both sides and voltage bases in the same ratio, $V_{B,H}/V_{B,L}=a$. Since $V_H=aV_L$,

$$
V_{H,pu}
=\frac{aV_L}{aV_{B,L}}
=V_{L,pu}.
$$ {#eq-pu-transformer-voltage-equality}

Current bases change inversely with voltage, as the winding currents do, so their per-unit values also match. Impedance bases satisfy $Z_{B,H}/Z_{B,L}=a^2$, and a physical impedance referred from the low side to the high side gains the same factor $a^2$:

$$
\frac{a^2\underline Z_L}{a^2 Z_{B,L}}
=\frac{\underline Z_L}{Z_{B,L}}.
$$ {#eq-pu-transformer-impedance-invariance}

The same per-unit impedance therefore appears from either winding. This holds only with a common power base and voltage bases that follow the transformer ratio; otherwise an off-nominal per-unit tap remains, as the [transformer $\pi$-model tutorial](transformer-pi-model.qmd) shows.

## 5. Change a per-unit base safely

A base change leaves the physical quantity unchanged, so equating $\underline Z_{pu,old}V_{B,old}^2/S_{B,old}$ with $\underline Z_{pu,new}V_{B,new}^2/S_{B,new}$ gives

$$
\underline Z_{pu,new}
=\underline Z_{pu,old}
\frac{S_{B,new}}{S_{B,old}}
\left(\frac{V_{B,old}}{V_{B,new}}\right)^2.
$$ {#eq-pu-impedance-base-change}

Admittance uses the reciprocal factors, while power and voltage follow directly from @eq-pu-definition:

$$
\underline Y_{pu,new}
=\underline Y_{pu,old}
\frac{S_{B,old}}{S_{B,new}}
\left(\frac{V_{B,new}}{V_{B,old}}\right)^2,
\qquad
\underline S_{pu,new}
=\underline S_{pu,old}\frac{S_{B,old}}{S_{B,new}},
\qquad
\underline V_{pu,new}
=\underline V_{pu,old}\frac{V_{B,old}}{V_{B,new}}.
$$ {#eq-pu-admittance-base-change}

::: {.callout-tip}
If a memorised base-change formula is in doubt, return to physical units and divide by the new base; slower, but the direction of every factor is then unambiguous.
:::

## 6. Worked example: four buses, three voltage zones

A generator at bus 1 feeds a load at bus 4 through a step-up transformer, a transmission line, and a step-down transformer, following the multi-zone procedure in [@grainger1994]. @fig-pu-four-bus shows the network and its nameplate data; the dashed boundaries through both transformers separate the three voltage zones.

![Single-line diagram of the four-bus example. Generator G at bus 1 feeds the load at bus 4 through step-up transformer T1, a $230\ \mathrm{kV}$ line with its charging susceptance split between both ends, and step-down transformer T2. Elements carry their nameplate ratings; dashed boundaries mark the voltage base propagated into each zone.](figures/generated/per-unit-four-bus-network.svg){#fig-pu-four-bus fig-align="center" width="100%"}

| Element | Rating | Impedance on its own rating |
|---|---|---|
| Generator G, bus 1 | $90\ \mathrm{MVA}$, $13.8\ \mathrm{kV}$ | $\mathrm{j}0.18$ p.u. (subtransient) |
| Transformer T1, buses 1--2 | $125\ \mathrm{MVA}$, $13.2/230\ \mathrm{kV}$ | $\mathrm{j}0.10$ p.u. |
| Line, buses 2--3 | $230\ \mathrm{kV}$ | $15+\mathrm{j}80\ \Omega$, total charging $4.22\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{S}$ |
| Transformer T2, buses 3--4 | $75\ \mathrm{MVA}$, $230/69\ \mathrm{kV}$ | $\mathrm{j}0.08$ p.u. |
| Load, bus 4 | --- | $60+\mathrm{j}25\ \mathrm{MVA}$ drawn at $66\ \mathrm{kV}$ |

: Network data before normalisation {#tbl-pu-network-data}

The system base is $100\ \mathrm{MVA}$ with $230\ \mathrm{kV}$ in the transmission zone. Two deliberate traps: the generator is rated $13.8\ \mathrm{kV}$ while the adjacent transformer winding is rated $13.2\ \mathrm{kV}$, and no element is rated at the system power base.

### Step 1: zone bases and equipment conversion

Voltage bases propagate through rated transformer ratios, never through the ratings of machines connected to a zone.

```{python}
#| label: lst-pu-zone-bases
#| lst-cap: "Propagate voltage bases across transformers and rebase every element"
#| code-summary: "Build zone bases and convert equipment data to the system base"

import numpy as np

S_BASE_MVA = 100.0
V_BASE_TRANSMISSION_KV = 230.0
T1_LV_RATED_KV, T1_HV_RATED_KV = 13.2, 230.0
T2_HV_RATED_KV, T2_LV_RATED_KV = 230.0, 69.0

v_base_ll_kv = {
    "generator": V_BASE_TRANSMISSION_KV * T1_LV_RATED_KV / T1_HV_RATED_KV,
    "transmission": V_BASE_TRANSMISSION_KV,
    "distribution": V_BASE_TRANSMISSION_KV * T2_LV_RATED_KV / T2_HV_RATED_KV,
}
z_base_ohm = {zone: kv**2 / S_BASE_MVA for zone, kv in v_base_ll_kv.items()}
i_base_ka = {
    zone: S_BASE_MVA / (np.sqrt(3.0) * kv) for zone, kv in v_base_ll_kv.items()
}


def change_impedance_base(
    z_pu_old: complex,
    s_base_old_mva: float,
    v_base_old_kv: float,
    s_base_new_mva: float,
    v_base_new_kv: float,
) -> complex:
    """Convert a per-unit impedance between power and voltage bases."""
    return (
        z_pu_old
        * (s_base_new_mva / s_base_old_mva)
        * (v_base_old_kv / v_base_new_kv) ** 2
    )


z_generator_pu = change_impedance_base(
    0.18j, 90.0, 13.8, S_BASE_MVA, v_base_ll_kv["generator"]
)
z_t1_pu = change_impedance_base(
    0.10j, 125.0, T1_LV_RATED_KV, S_BASE_MVA, v_base_ll_kv["generator"]
)
z_t2_pu = change_impedance_base(
    0.08j, 75.0, T2_LV_RATED_KV, S_BASE_MVA, v_base_ll_kv["distribution"]
)
z_line_pu = (15.0 + 80.0j) / z_base_ohm["transmission"]
y_line_half_pu = 0.5 * 4.22e-4j * z_base_ohm["transmission"]

for zone, kv in v_base_ll_kv.items():
    print(
        f"{zone:13s} V_B = {kv:7.3f} kV   "
        f"Z_B = {z_base_ohm[zone]:8.4f} ohm   I_B = {i_base_ka[zone]:7.4f} kA"
    )
print(f"generator  {z_generator_pu.imag:.6f}j p.u.")
print(f"T1         {z_t1_pu.imag:.6f}j p.u.")
print(f"line       {z_line_pu.real:.6f} {z_line_pu.imag:+.6f}j p.u.")
print(f"line b/2   {y_line_half_pu.imag:.6f}j p.u.")
print(f"T2         {z_t2_pu.imag:.6f}j p.u.")

# Rebasing a transformer from either winding must give the same result.
assert np.allclose(
    z_t1_pu,
    change_impedance_base(
        0.10j, 125.0, T1_HV_RATED_KV, S_BASE_MVA, v_base_ll_kv["transmission"]
    ),
)
assert np.allclose(
    z_t2_pu,
    change_impedance_base(
        0.08j, 75.0, T2_HV_RATED_KV, S_BASE_MVA, v_base_ll_kv["transmission"]
    ),
)
```

Both transformers keep voltage-base factors of exactly one because their windings define the zone bases; only the power ratio remains. The generator's $13.8\ \mathrm{kV}$ rating differs from the $13.2\ \mathrm{kV}$ zone base, so its reactance picks up the factor $(13.8/13.2)^2\approx1.093$ on top of $100/90$.

### Step 2: one voltage profile, two unit systems

Walking from the known load bus back to the generator gives the voltage and current at every bus. The same traversal function runs twice: on per-unit data, where every transformer ratio is one, and on physical data in phase-to-neutral kilovolts, kiloamperes, and ohms, where each transformer ratio and referred impedance must be handled explicitly.

```{python}
#| label: lst-pu-network-sweep
#| lst-cap: "Solve the same network in per unit and in physical units"
#| code-summary: "Sweep from the load to the source and compare both unit systems"

from typing import NamedTuple


class Branch(NamedTuple):
    """One step towards the source, with data referred to the arriving zone."""

    voltage_ratio: float  # unity for every branch of the per-unit model
    series_impedance: complex
    shunt_admittance_each_end: complex


def sweep_towards_source(
    voltage: complex, current: complex, branches: list[Branch]
) -> list[tuple[complex, complex]]:
    """Return the voltage and current at each bus from the load to the source."""
    profile = [(voltage, current)]
    for branch in branches:
        voltage *= branch.voltage_ratio
        current /= branch.voltage_ratio
        current += branch.shunt_admittance_each_end * voltage
        voltage += branch.series_impedance * current
        current += branch.shunt_admittance_each_end * voltage
        profile.append((voltage, current))
    return profile


s_load_mva = 60.0 + 25.0j
v_load_ll_kv = 66.0

voltage_pu = v_load_ll_kv / v_base_ll_kv["distribution"] + 0.0j
current_pu = np.conj(s_load_mva / S_BASE_MVA / voltage_pu)
profile_pu = sweep_towards_source(
    voltage_pu,
    current_pu,
    [
        Branch(1.0, z_t2_pu, 0.0),
        Branch(1.0, z_line_pu, y_line_half_pu),
        Branch(1.0, z_t1_pu, 0.0),
    ],
)

voltage_ln_kv = v_load_ll_kv / np.sqrt(3.0) + 0.0j
current_ka = np.conj(s_load_mva / (3.0 * voltage_ln_kv))
profile_physical = sweep_towards_source(
    voltage_ln_kv,
    current_ka,
    [
        Branch(T2_HV_RATED_KV / T2_LV_RATED_KV, 0.08j * T2_HV_RATED_KV**2 / 75.0, 0.0),
        Branch(1.0, 15.0 + 80.0j, 0.5 * 4.22e-4j),
        Branch(T1_LV_RATED_KV / T1_HV_RATED_KV, 0.10j * T1_LV_RATED_KV**2 / 125.0, 0.0),
    ],
)

bus_zones = [
    (4, "distribution"),
    (3, "transmission"),
    (2, "transmission"),
    (1, "generator"),
]
print(
    f"{'bus':>3} {'zone':>13} {'|V| p.u.':>9} "
    f"{'|V| kV(LL)':>11} {'|I| p.u.':>9} {'|I| A':>9}"
)
for (bus, zone), (v_pu, i_pu), (v_kv, i_ka) in zip(
    bus_zones, profile_pu, profile_physical
):
    print(
        f"{bus:>3} {zone:>13} {abs(v_pu):>9.4f} {abs(v_kv) * np.sqrt(3.0):>11.3f} "
        f"{abs(i_pu):>9.4f} {abs(i_ka) * 1e3:>9.1f}"
    )
    # Denormalising with each zone's own bases must reproduce the physical solution.
    assert np.allclose(v_pu * v_base_ll_kv[zone] / np.sqrt(3.0), v_kv)
    assert np.allclose(i_pu * i_base_ka[zone], i_ka)
```

The two calculations agree at every bus: the per-unit network contains no turns ratios, yet it reproduces a calculation that referred impedances and currents through them explicitly. In the printed profile, buses 3 and 4 carry the same per-unit current although the physical currents differ by the $230/69$ ratio, and the current changes between buses 3 and 2 only because the line charging injects reactive current. The $0.9565$ p.u. load voltage requires $1.048$ p.u. at the generator terminal, in every zone's terms.

### Step 3: back to physical amperes

Per-unit results must be denormalised with the bases of the zone where the quantity lives. For a bolted three-phase fault at bus 2, with the customary $1.0$ p.u. prefault voltage and no load-current contribution, the generator and T1 reactances are in series.

```{python}
#| label: lst-pu-fault-current
#| lst-cap: "Denormalise a fault current in the correct voltage zone"
#| code-summary: "Convert a per-unit fault current to kiloamperes"

z_thevenin_pu = z_generator_pu + z_t1_pu
i_fault_pu = 1.0 / z_thevenin_pu
i_fault_ka = abs(i_fault_pu) * i_base_ka["transmission"]

print(f"Thevenin reactance at bus 2 = {z_thevenin_pu.imag:.6f} p.u.")
print(f"fault current = {abs(i_fault_pu):.4f} p.u. = {i_fault_ka:.4f} kA")
print(f"short-circuit power = {S_BASE_MVA / abs(z_thevenin_pu):.2f} MVA")

# Cross-check in ohms, with both reactances referred to the 230 kV side.
x_generator_ohm = 0.18 * 13.8**2 / 90.0 * (T1_HV_RATED_KV / T1_LV_RATED_KV) ** 2
x_t1_ohm = 0.10 * T1_HV_RATED_KV**2 / 125.0
i_fault_ohmic_ka = (
    V_BASE_TRANSMISSION_KV / np.sqrt(3.0) / (x_generator_ohm + x_t1_ohm)
)
assert np.allclose(i_fault_ka, i_fault_ohmic_ka)
```

The ohmic cross-check reaches the same kiloamperes only because the generator reactance is first referred through T1, which is where the $(13.8/13.2)^2$ factor of Step 1 comes from. Using $I_B$ of the generator zone would overstate the fault current by the factor $230/13.2$. Two instructive changes: set the transformer LV rating to $13.8\ \mathrm{kV}$ and the generator conversion factor collapses to $100/90$; raise the load voltage towards $69\ \mathrm{kV}$ and the required generator-terminal voltage falls.

## 7. Common mistakes

- **Confusing the base with the actual value.** The voltage base is a selected reference, often equal to nominal voltage; the operating voltage varies around it.
- **Mixing three-phase and per-phase conventions.** Pair total $S_B$ with line-to-line $V_B$, or per-phase power with line-to-neutral voltage.
- **Forgetting the manufacturer's base.** Nameplate percentages are on the equipment rating and must be rebased before combining with network quantities.
- **Applying the impedance factor to admittance.** The two scale reciprocally; use @eq-pu-admittance-base-change or convert through siemens.
- **Propagating voltage bases from machine ratings.** Only transformer rated ratios propagate the base; a wrong zone introduces squared errors in impedance.
- **Expecting per unit to fix numerical problems.** Singular topology, poor observability, and bad parameters remain modelling problems.

## 8. Takeaways

- A per-unit value is an actual quantity divided by a declared base, and it is meaningless without that base.
- Choosing total $S_B$ and line-to-line $V_B$ determines $I_B$, $Z_B$, and $Y_B$, and preserves the forms of Ohm's law and the complex-power equation.
- One system-wide power base plus voltage bases propagated through rated transformer ratios removes nominal turns ratios from the network model.
- Impedance rebasing scales with the new power base and inversely with the squared new voltage base; admittance does the opposite.
- Equipment rated at a voltage different from its zone base, such as a generator behind a step-up transformer, needs both factors of @eq-pu-impedance-base-change.
- Denormalising a result requires the bases of the zone in which that quantity physically exists.
